content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 142 of the Constitution of India is titled “Enforcement of decrees and orders of the Supreme Court and orders as to discovery, etc”. It forms an integral component of The Union (Articles 52–151), located within the “The Union” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) The Supreme Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament and, until provision in that behalf is so made, in such manner as the President may by order1 prescribe.

(2) Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Supreme Court shall, as respects the whole of the territory of India, have all and every power to make any order for the purpose of securing the attendance of any person, the discovery or production of any documents, or the investigation or punishment of any contempt of itself.

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 142 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. It regulates executive, legislative, or fundamental citizen interests to maintain the rule of law and constitutional supremacy.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) The Supreme Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament and, until provision in that behalf is so made, in such manner as the President may by order1 prescribe.
2. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Supreme Court shall, as respects the whole of the territory of India, have all and every power to make any order for the purpose of securing the attendance of any person, the discovery or production of any documents, or the investigation or punishment of any contempt of itself.

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 142 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

1. Scrutinize the constitutional source of power: Does Article 142 grant plenary power, or is it conditioned by express safeguards, legislative competence, or fundamental rights?
2. Apply the doctrine of ultra vires and manifest arbitrariness: If the directive creates arbitrary exceptions or bypasses statutory provisions, it violates Article 14 and the mandate of Article 142.

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 142 (Enforcement of decrees and orders of the Supreme Court and orders as to discovery, etc) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 142 is situated in The Union (Articles 52–151), governing the “The Union” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) The Supreme Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament and, until provision in that behalf is so made, in such manner as the President may by order1 prescribe.
2. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Supreme Court shall, as respects the whole of the territory of India, have all and every power to make any order for the purpose of securing the attendance of any person, the discovery or production of any documents, or the investigation or punishment of any contempt of itself.

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 142:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 142 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 142 of the Constitution of India, titled “Enforcement of decrees and orders of the Supreme Court and orders as to discovery, etc”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The Union (Articles 52–151), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 142 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) The Supreme Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament and, until provision in that behalf is so made, in such manner as the President may by order1 prescribe.
(a) Limb 2: (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Supreme Court shall, as respects the whole of the territory of India, have all and every power to make any order for the purpose of securing the attendance of any person, the discovery or production of any documents, or the investigation or punishment of any contempt of itself.
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 142 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 142 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 142:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 142;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 142 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 142?
Rule: Under Article 142, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 142 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: Article 142(1) empowers the Supreme Court to pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it. Any decree or order so passed is enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as may be prescribed by Parliament or by Presidential order. It represents the inherent equitable reservoir of the apex court, enabling it to transcend procedural rigidities to achieve substantive justice.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Justice is higher than mere technical legality. Article 142 equips the Supreme Court with an extraordinary, non-statutory power to fashion novel remedies and fill legislative vacuums to ensure that procedural hurdles do not thwart complete substantive justice, provided it does not disregard express statutory prohibitions or basic constitutional tenets.

Article 142 of the Constitution of India (Clauses 1 and 2)
Complemented by Article 129 (Court of Record & Contempt) and Article 141 (Binding Law)

essentialIngredients: Pendente Lite Jurisdiction: Operates 'in any cause or matter pending before it' — requires an existing judicial proceeding before the Court.
Objective Benchmark: Order must be necessary for doing 'complete justice' between the parties or in the public interest.
Universal Territorial Enforceability: Enforceable throughout the territory of India in the manner prescribed by law or by the President.

Ancillary Procedural Powers (Clause 2): Complete power to make orders for: (a) Securing attendance of any person; (b) Discovery or production of documents; (c) Investigation or punishment of any contempt of itself.

Substantive Limitations (SCBA v. Union of India): (1) Cannot supplant substantive statutory law; (2) Cannot build a new edifice where the legislature explicitly prohibits it; (3) Cannot punish an advocate for contempt by suspending their statutory license under the Advocates Act, 1961.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 142 is the ultimate equitable engine of the Supreme Court of India.

### 1. The Scope of 'Complete Justice'
In *Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India (1991)* (Bhopal Gas Disaster), a Constitution Bench examined the outer limits of Article 142:
> *'The power under Article 142 is in its nature entirely of a different level. It is a constitutional power plenary in nature, and is not restricted by statutory limitations. The power is given to the highest court of the land to do complete justice, and is uninhibited by statutory provisions.'*
Under this power, the Court sanctioned the $470 million mass settlement and quashed criminal prosecutions (later revoked in review).

### 2. The Constitutional Re-anchoring: Supreme Court Bar Association (1998)
In *Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998)*, a 5-judge bench tempered the sweeping assertions of Union Carbide:
- **Cannot Supplant Substantive Law:** Article 142 is a curative power designed to build upon and supplement statutory law, not to override express statutory prohibitions.
- **Contempt & Professional Misconduct:** The Court held that while Article 129 empowers it to punish for contempt, Article 142 cannot be used to suspend an advocate's license to practice, because that power is vested exclusively in the Bar Council under the Advocates Act, 1961.

### 3. Landmark Modern Applications
- **Ayodhya Dispute (M. Siddiq v. Suresh Das, 2019):** A 5-judge bench invoked Article 142 to allot 5 acres of land to the Sunni Central Waqf Board for a mosque to achieve complete, holistic justice while granting the disputed site for a temple.
- **Irretrievable Breakdown of Marriage (Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan, 2023):** A 5-judge Constitution Bench held that the Supreme Court can grant a divorce on the ground of 'irretrievable breakdown of marriage' under Article 142, and can waive the mandatory statutory 6-month cooling-off period under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
examples: Waiving Matrimonial Cooling-Off Period: A husband and wife have lived separately in hostile litigation for 12 years. They file for mutual consent divorce under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act and pray to waive the 6-month cooling-off period. Applying Shilpa Sailesh, the Supreme Court invokes Article 142 to dissolve the marriage immediately, holding that compelling estranged couples to wait when the marriage is dead is cruelty and antithetical to complete justice.

Overriding Procedural Deadlocks: During a national medical emergency, life-saving imported drugs are held up at ports due to conflicting jurisdictional claims between two state licensing tribunals. On an Article 32 petition, the Supreme Court invokes Article 142 to order the immediate nationwide release of the drugs under an ad-hoc central monitoring committee, overriding statutory boundary disputes.
distinctions: Article 142 vs Article 136: Article 136 is an appellate jurisdictional gateway granting special leave to appeal; Article 142 is a substantive remedial power empowering the Court to pass any decree or order necessary for complete justice once seized of a matter.

Supplementing Law vs Supplanting Law: Article 142 can supplement or fill legislative vacuums where statutes are silent (e.g., Vishaka guidelines); it cannot directly supplant or violate express statutory prohibitions (Supreme Court Bar Association).
problemApplication: Issue: An advocate is found guilty of criminal contempt of court for scandalizing the bench. The Supreme Court imposes a fine and, in purported exercise of Article 142, passes an order suspending the advocate's license to practice law for 3 years. Is the suspension of license valid?

Rule: In Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India (1998), a Constitution Bench held that Article 142 cannot be used to usurp powers statutorily vested in professional regulatory bodies under the Advocates Act, 1961.

Application: While the Supreme Court can punish for contempt under Article 129 (imprisonment or fine), suspending a license to practice falls exclusively within the domain of the State Bar Council and Bar Council of India under the Advocates Act.
Counterargument: The Court asserts that complete justice requires protecting the majesty of the court from contumacious advocates.
Conclusion: Under the binding SCBA doctrine, the order suspending the advocate's license is ultra vires Article 142 and impermissible.
